extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, federal litigators, and judges (practitioners litigating patent §101 and jurisdictional motions in the Court of Federal Claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and tests a court uses to resolve motions to dismiss (RCFC 12(b)(1) and 12(b)(6)) in patent litigation, including jurisdictional doctrines (ACA, §1498(c), preclusion) and the Alice/Mayo two-step framework for patent-eligibility and inventive-concept analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: RCFC 12(b)(1) jurisdictional burden and standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When a challenge is mounted pursuant to RCFC 12(b)(1), plaintiff bears the burden of establishing this court’s subject-matter jurisdiction by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reviewing allegations in support of jurisdiction, the court must presume all undisputed facts are true and construe all reasonable inferences in plaintiff’s favor (Scheuer). If the motion challenges the truth of jurisdictional facts, the court may consider relevant evidence to resolve the factual dispute (Reynolds). If the court determines it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, it must dismiss the complaint (RCFC 12(h)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: RCFC 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss standard (pleading/merits)
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive a motion to dismiss under RCFC 12(b)(6), a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court presumes facts as alleged and makes all reasonable inferences in favor of the plaintiff; however, the court is not required to accept asserted legal conclusions (Iqbal/Twombly). A complaint should be dismissed when the facts asserted do not entitle the claimant to a legal remedy. The court may consider allegations in the complaint, exhibits attached, matters incorporated by reference, public records of which it may take judicial notice, and documents central to the complaint (Dimare Fresh; Terry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3727) jurisdictional test
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACA prohibits assignment of a claim against the United States unless the claim is allowed, the amount decided, and a warrant for payment issued; it applies to assignment of patent claims for past infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary assignments of patent claims are ineffective against the government unless they qualify for judicially-recognized exceptions or do not run afoul of the Act's purposes. An important exception is where assignments are to an 'alter-ego' and the same individual possessed equitable ownership (MDS Assocs.; Ideal Innovations). If the inventor is effectively the same claimant (e.g., ninety-percent owner, president, CEO), the ACA may not bar suits for pre-assignment infringements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 28 U.S.C. §1498(c) and foreign-activity jurisdictional boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1498(c) provides that patent claims against the United States do not extend to 'any claim arising in a foreign country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: § 1498(c) does not apply where the alleged infringing activities took place within the United States. Allegations that accused products were manufactured in the United States (even if later used abroad) can be sufficient to establish the court's jurisdiction (Zoltek). The court draws reasonable inferences in plaintiff's favor if jurisdictional facts are not challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preclusion from prior litigation as a jurisdictional/merits issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be precluded if previously litigated and dismissed with prejudice against the same accused products or actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether preclusion applies depends on factual allegations showing the accused products were manufactured/sold by the same entity previously sued. Bare assertions by a defendant are insufficient on a motion to dismiss; the court presumes undisputed facts in plaintiff’s favor and requires more specific evidence or allegations to find preclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework for patent-eligible subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: First, determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas). If so, second, determine whether the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, supply an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry looks to the 'focus' or character of the claim as a whole (Elec. Power Grp.; Enfish). If directed to an ineligible concept, the court asks whether additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (Alice; Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Directed to' / focus-of-the-claim inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The court must consider the asserted patent claims 'in their entirety to ascertain whether their character as a whole is directed to excluded subject matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court asks what the patent asserts to be the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art to determine whether the claim’s character as a whole is directed to an ineligible concept (ChargePoint; Simio). Look to claim language, specification disclosures, and what the patent describes as its advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept standard (step two of Alice)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'inventive concept' is an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a claim on the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive concept must be more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously known to the industry (Affinity Labs; Mayo). Implementation of a known technique with particular devices in a specific combination can be inventive if plausibly alleged (Cellspin). If the only inventive concept is the application of an abstract idea using conventional techniques, the claim remains ineligible (BSG Tech).

rubrics_metrics.name: When §101 can be decided on a motion to dismiss
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under §101 is a question of law that may involve underlying questions of fact; the court may determine eligibility on a motion to dismiss only when there are no factual allegations that, taken as true, prevent resolving the eligibility question as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues material to §101 exist, the court cannot resolve eligibility at the 12(b)(6) stage (Berkheimer; Aatrix; Simio). Conversely, where the 'character as a whole' of the claims is clear from the pleadings and patent documents, the court may rule as a matter of law (e.g., CardioNet, Univ. of Fla. examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading requirement for alleging an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive a motion to dismiss, a plaintiff must plead plausible and specific factual allegations that aspects of the claim are inventive rather than merely label techniques as inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boilerplate conclusory assertions or labels are insufficient. Plaintiff should identify specific technical improvements or non-conventional combinations and allege facts suggesting these techniques had not been implemented in a similar way (Cellspin). Specificity about how claimed elements improve technological functioning supports survival of a motion to dismiss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of preemption and public-policy concerns in §101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena are excluded from patent protection because they are basic tools of scientific and technological work and monopolizing them might impede innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate the risk of preemption (i.e., whether the claim would monopolize an abstract idea) as part of the §101 inquiry. Demonstrations that claims would preempt the basic tools of innovation weigh against eligibility (Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of disputed vs. undisputed jurisdictional facts
rubrics_metrics.description: If jurisdictional facts are undisputed, courts presume them true and construe in plaintiff's favor; if defendant specifically challenges the truth of jurisdictional facts, the court may consider evidence outside the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When jurisdictional facts are not challenged, the court accepts plaintiff's allegations (Scheuer). When challenged, the court may resolve factual disputes by considering relevant evidence (Reynolds). This affects whether the court will dismiss for lack of jurisdiction under RCFC 12(b)(1).
